item.description:
A fix for 0.7.0, and it is the reason to update now.

The close button was closing windows nobody asked it to

Reported within an hour of 0.7.0 shipping: windows closing on their own while triggering, whole apps disappearing, one of them while the reporter was typing the message. If you are on 0.7.0, this is worth updating for today.

The close × introduced in 0.7.0 had its hit area *on* the slot rather than beside it — centred exactly on the tile's corner, so the top-right of every slot was a close button. Aiming in MiddleRing is by direction and the cursor never has to touch a slot, but nothing on screen says that: a parked ring puts tiles in front of you and tiles are what look clickable. So the cursor went onto them, and the click landed on the button.

With the default content setting every slot is an *app*, and closing an app slot closes every window that app has, at once. That is why it read as a whole session vanishing rather than one window going.

Three things now stand between a cursor and a closed window instead of one: the button sits outside the tile rather than on its corner, its hit area is smaller, and it does nothing at all until the cursor has been still on it for a fifth of a second. It only turns red once it is armed, so what it looks like and what a click will do are the same thing.

It logged you out instead of going to sleep

The worse half of the same report, and a much older bug than the button above.

When the ring decides not to open — the machine is going to sleep, the front app is on your exception list, nothing passed the screen filter — it used to let the trigger through to whatever else wanted it. That is right for a mouse button: a middle click that opens nothing should still open a tab. Applied to a keyboard shortcut it handed your own binding to macOS, and macOS owns a lot of them. ⇧⌘Q logs out. ⌃⌘Q locks the screen. ⌥⌘⎋ force-quits.

Sleeping is one of the moments the ring refuses. So a Mac that logged out instead of sleeping, closing every app on the way, was doing exactly what it had been asked — by a keystroke this app decided not to keep.

A keyboard trigger is now swallowed whether or not the ring opens. You bound it to MiddleRing; it belongs to MiddleRing even when MiddleRing has nothing to show. Mouse buttons and trackpad gestures still pass through, for the reason they always did.

That is not the whole answer, because the app is not always running — a paused or quit MiddleRing hands the shortcut back. So the trigger editor now warns you by name if you bind one the system already owns.

A click could stick after using the ring

Older, and it leaked outside the app. After acting on a slot with a right-click, the next click you made anywhere could lose its mouse-up — leaving the app underneath in a stuck drag or a selection that would not let go. Fixed.

Also

  • The settings text for the right-click actions said "the window you are aiming at". On an app slot that is every window the app has. It now says so, which matters most for the close action: it fires on press, with no delay, and the whole wedge of that slot is its target.
  • Resuming from Pause could quietly fail if Accessibility had been revoked, leaving the menu offering to pause something that was not running.
  • Solo's undo record was written on one thread and read on another.
  • The parked ring's hint in the centre disc was truncated in English.

Requirements

macOS 14 or later, Apple Silicon. MiddleRing needs Accessibility permission — that is what lets it read the window list and bring a window forward. Screen Recording is only requested if you turn live previews on.

Install

If you are on 0.3.0 or later this arrives on its own. Otherwise open the DMG, drag MiddleRing to Applications, launch it, and grant Accessibility when asked. It lives in the menu bar; there is no Dock icon.

Signed with a Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple, so it opens without a Gatekeeper warning.

The ring stopped working after the Mac woke up. It does not any more — and there is a close button on the slot you are aiming at.

It went deaf after sleeping

Reported as "it works until the Mac sleeps, then some apps trigger it and some do not, and quitting and reopening fixes it". Three causes, which is why it looked so inconsistent.

The one that made it stick: a display that dozes on its own and a machine that really sleeps announce themselves with different notifications, and only one of each pair is ever sent. MiddleRing raised its "nothing may be drawn" flag on one and lowered it on the other, so a display that slept by itself left the flag up forever and every trigger after that was refused. Restarting cleared it, which is exactly what you saw.

Why it looked app-dependent: the ring filters windows by which screen they are on, using frames it caches — and a display waking or being re-attached moves every window without telling anyone. The cached frames then belong to an arrangement that no longer exists, the per-screen filter drops all of them, and the ring refuses to open for the apps on that display and no others. The cache is now rebuilt on wake and whenever the screen arrangement changes.

And the input tap itself can come back from a sleep attached to something the system has already let go of, looking healthy by every quick check and hearing nothing. It is now tested properly and rebuilt rather than nudged.

None of the three said anything while failing, because every way the ring can decline to open looks the same from outside — the trigger fires and nothing happens. Each one now writes its reason to /tmp/middlering-ring.log.

A close button on the slot

Park the ring — a quick tap rather than a hold — and the slot you are aiming at grows a small × on its corner. Move onto it and click: that window closes and the ring stays up for the next one. On an app slot it closes every window that app has, which is what picking the app rather than one window has always meant here. A slot with nothing to close never grows one.

It presses the window's own close button rather than sending ⌘W, so an app with unsaved work asks about it exactly as it would have if you had reached for the window yourself.

Only on a parked ring, and that is deliberate. The corner sits about 10° off the slot's own direction — inside the sector that slot owns — so a flick aimed a little wide passes straight through it, and letting go there would close the window you were reaching for. Parking is the difference between a hand throwing the cursor and a hand placing it. In "hold and release" mode the ring never parks, so the × never appears; the right-click action is the way to close from there.

Settings › Trigger › Kapat düğmesi switches it off.

The name in the hub stops jumping

It used to be the first line of a centred stack, so every line that appeared underneath pushed it up and every line that left dropped it back — stepping between two slots where one has a subtitle and the other does not made the name move on every step. It now holds a fixed place in the middle and everything else hangs below it.

Those lines can also go entirely: Settings › Görünüm › **Ortadaki dairede ad altı satırlar**. That is the app name under a window title and the `tıkla seç · esc iptal` reminder. Worth saying once, not worth saying under every slot you step through.

The disc in the middle of the ring is sizeable now.

A smaller hub

Reported as too big, which it was for anyone who wanted the ring to take up less room — the hub was the one part of it that could not be changed. Settings › Görünüm › Ölçüler › Ortadaki daire, 64 to 170 points.

The catch is that the hub carries type drawn for exactly one size. Shrinking the disc and leaving the label alone overflows it, so everything inside now shrinks with the disc. There is a floor past which the label stops being readable, and a hub too small to read is worse than one slightly overfull.

At the small end the hub sits inside the deadzone. That is fine: the band between them already shows the pointer with nothing selected, and already turns red to say that letting go there closes the ring.

Fixes a ring slot that did nothing.

What was broken

Open an app from the ring, close it with the red button so it keeps living in the Dock, then pick it from the ring again — and nothing happens. Reported against pinned apps.

Two causes. Committing a pinned slot from the window ring went through the path that switches to an app rather than the one that knows how to start it: merging quick access into the window ring in 0.5.0 added the slot and did not connect it. In its own ring it worked.

The second is older, and is why this reproduced for some people and not others. The window list is rebuilt when apps launch, quit, activate or hide — and closing a window is none of those. So a slot can be holding a window that shut minutes ago with nothing having said so. Raising it fails quietly, the app comes to the front with no window, and from your side the slot did nothing at all.

Whether you hit it depended on whether anything else happened to refresh the list in between.

What it does now

Bringing a windowless app to the front and leaving it windowless is the wrong move. What clicking the Dock icon sends is a reopen, and a reopen is what makes an app produce a window — so that is what a slot with nothing behind it does.

Knowing when there is nothing behind it turned out to be the hard part. The window server reports six windows for a TextEdit showing one document, so counting them settles nothing. The ring stops guessing: it raises what it has, then checks a moment later whether a window actually appeared, and opens the app if none did.

Also

  • A pinned app takes its windows from everything open rather than from whatever the ring was about to draw, so a pin on another display still switches to it instead of opening a second window.
  • make test-activation walks these states and prints pass or fail, including the risk the new approach carries: reopening an app that already has a window leaves it with exactly one.

The two rings that offered the same apps now know about each other, and a pinned app can look like whatever you want it to.

Pins in the window ring

Quick access can hold the front of the window ring as well — of every page, not just the first. The direction to a pin is then the same on the third page as on the first, which is the entire point of pinning something.

A pinned app that happens to be running is taken out of the window list and given that app's windows, so the pin is the same slot the switcher would have shown, in a place that does not move, rather than a second slot for the same app. Its fan still opens.

Off by default. Pins spend slots that would otherwise show windows, and Settings states the trade with your own numbers rather than in the abstract: how many slots the pins take on each page and how many are left for windows.

Pins can carry their own icon

An SF Symbol, an emoji, or an image file. Leave it and you get the app's own icon, which is the right answer nearly always.

Image files are copied into the app's support folder rather than remembered by path. Remembering the path is the obvious thing, and the obvious thing turns a ring slot blank the first time you tidy your Downloads folder, for reasons nothing on screen can explain.

The shortcut rows gained image upload at the same time — they share the picker.

Fixed

  • Pinned slots read "Opera.app" if you have Finder set to show every extension, while the same app in the window ring read "Opera". The bundle's own name is used now, so the two agree.
  • The page dots miscounted once pins were at the front, because the page count was being worked out from how many slots were on screen.
  • --demo built its own slots and skipped the merge, which made the one way to look at this feature the one way that did not have it.

The ring now says when letting go will close it, and the plates behind the icons are optional.

The centre says what it does

Releasing with the cursor in the middle has always cancelled. Nothing said so. The ring used its accent colour to mean "this is what you are about to pick" and had no way to say "this is what you are about to *not* pick", so the safest thing you could do looked exactly like doing nothing.

It turns red now — the hub, the pointer, and the label, which reads Kapat. Three channels rather than one: colour alone is not a message to anyone who does not see red as red.

Only after you have aimed at something at least once, or once the ring is parked. The ring opens with the cursor already in the middle, and a warning that fires every single time is one you learn to ignore.

Bare icons

Görünüm can take the material plate out from behind the icons. What is left is the icon and a shadow — depth without a panel — and the icon grows into the space the plate used to take up.

Selection survives it as a tight ring of accent light around the icon itself. Window previews keep their plate: the image is clipped to it, and a photograph with no edge bleeds into anything light behind it.

Settings that say what they do

Görünüm needed this most. Three sliders labelled with words that described the implementation rather than the effect, and nothing explaining any of them. They are grouped now, every control has a line saying what it changes, and "Ölü bölge" is "Merkez boşluğu".

Elsewhere: a modifier on a trackpad gesture now says that it is a requirement, not a bonus — left unsaid, the first thing it does is make the gesture look broken to whoever set it and forgot. The Screen Recording note links to the permission instead of reciting the path to it. The shortcut rows have column headings.

Updating

If you are on 0.3.0 this one arrives on its own — MiddleRing checks for itself now. 0.2.0 and earlier still need one manual install, after which they are on the same footing.

Two more rings, a third thing right-click can do, trackpad gestures that take modifiers — and, from this version on, MiddleRing updates itself.

Quick access ring

A fixed list of apps in the order you put them in. The switcher is ordered by recency, which is the right answer for switching and the wrong one for muscle memory; this ring never moves, so the direction is learnable.

A pinned app that is closed keeps its slot, shows a dimmed icon, and launches when you commit it. One that has been uninstalled leaves the ring rather than sitting there failing.

App shortcut ring

Keystrokes for whichever app is in front, under names you gave them. Open it in Figma and you get Figma's; open it in a browser and you get the browser's. Committing a slot posts that keystroke straight to the app.

A slot shows the keystroke by default — using the ring is how you stop needing it — or a symbol picked from a short grid of SF Symbols and emoji, which is quicker to pick out of a circle at speed. A "global" set sits under whatever the frontmost app contributes, so the ring is not empty in an app you have not got round to configuring.

Solo

Right-click a slot to minimize everything that does not belong to that app and switch to it. App-level even when you aimed at a single window: "leave me with this one" means the app you are about to work in.

A second solo on the same app restores exactly what the first one minimized — not everything currently minimized, which would also undo whatever you had tidied away yourself.

Trackpad gestures take modifiers

Kept separate from a ring's keyboard and mouse modifiers, so binding a ring to ⌃⌥⌘L does not silently demand ⌃⌥⌘ on its finger gesture too.

That also makes two fingers bindable. On its own it is the system's secondary click and taking that from every app is not a setting anyone would look for again; under ⌃ or ⌥ it is a gesture nothing else claims.

It updates itself now

The hard part of updating was never noticing that a new version exists — it is replacing a running app in place with its Developer ID signature intact, and getting that wrong costs you the Accessibility grant along with the app. So this uses Sparkle, and the update feed is signed with a key whose private half never leaves the developer's machine.

This is the last version you have to install by hand. 0.2.0 shipped without an updater, so it cannot pull this one down; from 0.3.0 onward MiddleRing checks for itself and offers the update in place. There is a "Check for updates" item in the menu bar and a switch in Settings › Genel if you would rather it did not.

Also

  • Rings are a list internally rather than two hand-copied blocks of settings, so the next one costs an enum case. Triggers you had already chosen are migrated; nothing needs re-binding.
  • Fixed: nested Sparkle components failed notarization on the first attempt, which is worth saying out loud because codesign --deep --strict passes on exactly that mistake.
